q.q: Which two ideas sum up the purpose of an operating system?
o: Managing the computer's resources, and providing an interface between hardware, applications and user
Translating source code into machine code, and managing the computer's memory and processor
Protecting the computer from malware, and backing up the user's files at regular intervals
Running the start-up routine from ROM, and storing all programs permanently on the disk
q.why: An OS manages processor time, memory, storage, devices and files, and acts as the go-between for hardware, applications and the user.

q.q: In the four-part model of an operating system, which component allocates memory, secondary storage and processor time?
o: User interface
Kernel
Application interface
Hardware interface
q.why: The kernel is the core: it loads and removes programs and allocates memory, storage and processor time.

q.q: In the four-part model of an operating system, where are device drivers held?
o: Kernel
User interface
Application interface
Hardware interface
q.why: The application interface offers services that programs call and holds the drivers that let the OS talk to each device.

q.q: A word processor asks the operating system to save a file. Which component of the four-part model provides this service?
o: User interface
Hardware interface
Kernel
Application interface
q.why: Programs call OS services through the application interface; the user interface faces the person, not the programs.

q.q: Why will a version of Windows built for x86 processors not run unchanged on an ARM-based phone?
o: The OS issues machine-code instructions for one particular processor family
The phone's licence agreement forbids installing a desktop operating system
Device drivers are stored in the kernel and cannot be copied between devices
The ARM phone stores its operating system in ROM, which cannot be overwritten
q.why: Each OS is built for a processor family's instruction set, so a different family needs a different build.

q.q: Why would computers be harder to program without an operating system?
o: Programs could not be written in high-level languages without an operating system
Every program would need its own code to control every possible disk, screen and printer
Programs would have to be translated by an interpreter rather than a compiler
Every program would have to be stored in ROM rather than on secondary storage
q.why: The OS provides shared services and drivers, so applications never need to drive the hardware directly.

q.q: Where is a single user, single application operating system mainly found today?
o: On smartphones and tablets, where one person signs in at a time
On mainframes that serve thousands of users at once
In simple embedded controllers, such as a basic microwave
On web servers that handle many visitors' requests
q.why: Single-application OSs are small and simple, so they suit basic embedded devices (and early systems like MS-DOS).

q.q: A tablet lets its owner stream music while browsing the Web. Which type of operating system is this?
o: Multi-user
Single user, single application
Batch processing
Single user, multitasking
q.why: One person has several programs running at once; phones and tablets normally have one user signed in.

q.q: What does time-slicing achieve in a multi-user operating system?
o: Each user's task runs on its own separate processor core, so no user ever has to wait
Memory is divided into equal fixed-size pages so that each user gets the same amount
Each user is given the CPU for a fixed hour of the day according to a booking timetable
Each user's task gets a very short turn on the CPU, so every user seems to have the machine to themselves
q.why: Rapid, rotating short turns share the processor fairly and give the impression of exclusive use.

q.q: Which feature is essential in a multi-user operating system but not needed in a single user one?
o: A graphical user interface with windows and icons
Keeping each user's files private from the other users
Device drivers for printers and other peripherals
Allocating memory to each program as it is loaded
q.why: Many users share one machine, so accounts, passwords and access rights must keep each user's data private.

q.q: A school network lets 30 pupils log on to 30 separate PCs. Why is this not, by itself, an example of a multi-user operating system?
o: The pupils do not all run the same application at exactly the same time as each other
A multi-user operating system must use a command line rather than a graphical interface
Each pupil uses a different computer, not one computer's processor and memory shared at the same time
A multi-user operating system can only be used by a maximum of ten people at once
q.why: The defining feature is many users sharing one computer's processor and memory simultaneously.

q.q: In a multiprogramming system with one CPU, how many programs execute at any single instant?
o: One
All the programs held in memory
One for each user logged on
Two, one in each half of memory
q.why: Several programs are resident in memory, but a single processor executes only one at a time.

q.q: In multiprogramming, when does the OS typically switch the CPU to another program?
o: When the running program has to wait, for example for an input/output operation
Only when the running program has finished completely and been removed from memory
Whenever a second processor core becomes free to take on the extra work
Every time the user clicks on a different window on the desktop
q.why: Switching on I/O waits keeps the processor busy rather than idle.

q.q: What is the main benefit of multiprocessing?
o: Lower memory use, because programs share a single copy of their code and data
Better security, because each user's data is held on a different processor
Speed, because instructions genuinely execute at the same time on different processors
Fewer device drivers, because each processor controls only its own devices
q.why: Multiprocessing uses two or more processors or cores for true parallel processing.

q.q: Which term describes several paths of execution inside one process that share its memory and code?
o: Multiprogramming
Multithreading
Multiprocessing
Time-slicing
q.why: A thread is a separate path of execution; all the threads of a process share its memory and code.

q.q: Why can a web server handle hundreds of visitors efficiently using threads?
o: Each request is sent to a separate physical processor in the server
A separate copy of the server program is loaded for each visitor
Requests are collected and processed together in an overnight batch
Each request gets its own thread within one copy of the server program
q.why: Threads share the process's code and memory, so hundreds of copies of the program are not needed.

q.q: Two threads each hold a file and wait for the file the other one holds. What has occurred?
o: Thrashing
Deadlock
Time-slicing
Starvation by shortest job first
q.why: Each waits for the other for ever, which is a deadlock.

q.q: Which is a risk of multithreading?
o: Two threads updating the same shared value at once can corrupt it
Each thread needs its own copy of the program, using a lot of memory
Threads can only run on separate computers linked by a network
A process is limited to one thread, so work cannot be divided
q.why: Threads share data, so simultaneous updates can corrupt it and resource waits can cause deadlock.

q.q: Which statement correctly compares multitasking on one core with multiprocessing?
o: Multitasking gives true parallel execution; multiprocessing only appears simultaneous on one core
Both give true parallel execution, but multitasking needs at least two processors to work
Neither gives parallel execution; both simply hold several programs in memory at once
Multitasking only appears simultaneous on one core; multiprocessing gives true parallel execution
q.why: On one core only one task executes at any instant; with several processors, work genuinely runs at once.

q.q: Which is NOT one of the jobs of memory management?
o: Allocating memory to a program when it is loaded
Protecting each program's memory from other programs
Translating each program into machine code before it runs
Reclaiming memory when a program ends
q.why: Memory management allocates, protects, reclaims and extends memory; translation is done by compilers, interpreters and assemblers.

q.q: Which is true of paging?
o: Memory is divided into variable-sized blocks that follow the program's structure
Each program must be stored in one continuous block of physical memory
Memory is divided into equal, fixed-size blocks mapped to frames by a page table
Page boundaries are placed between subroutines so that each fits exactly
q.why: Paging is a physical division into equal pages; segments are the variable, logical units.

q.q: What does a segment table store for each segment?
o: A base address and a length
A page number and a frame number only
The segment's colour depth and size
The owner's password and access rights
q.why: Segments vary in size, so the table needs where each starts and how long it is.

q.q: Which type of wasted space is associated with paging?
o: External fragmentation: gaps left between variable-sized blocks
Disk thrashing: pages constantly swapped between RAM and disk
Deadlock: two programs each waiting for memory held by the other
Internal fragmentation: the unused part of a program's last page
q.why: Programs rarely fill their last fixed-size page, wasting space inside it; gaps between segments are external fragmentation.

q.q: Which pair correctly contrasts paging and segmentation?
o: Pages are logical units of variable size; segments are a physical division of fixed size
Pages are a physical division of fixed size; segments are logical units of variable size
Pages need contiguous memory; segments can be scattered anywhere in RAM
Pages are used for virtual memory; segments are only used on solid state drives
q.why: Paging ignores program structure; segmentation follows it, e.g. a subroutine or the stack.

q.q: What is virtual memory?
o: Using secondary storage to extend RAM by moving out data that is not currently needed
Using spare cache memory inside the processor to hold the whole operating system
Splitting a program into logical segments of different sizes held in a segment table
Holding copies of web pages on a proxy server to save bandwidth for users
q.why: When RAM is full, pages not currently needed are swapped out to disk.

q.q: A computer with too little RAM runs very slowly as pages are constantly swapped between RAM and disk. What is this called?
o: Deadlock
Fragmentation
Spooling
Disk thrashing
q.why: Constant swapping of pages in and out of virtual memory slows the computer dramatically.

q.q: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process a fixed time slice in turn, sending unfinished processes to the back of the queue?
o: First come, first served
Round robin
Shortest job first
Priority scheduling
q.why: Round robin rotates through the processes with a fixed quantum.

q.q: Which scheduling algorithm risks a long job never being run if short jobs keep arriving?
o: First come, first served
Round robin
Shortest job first
Priority scheduling by arrival time
q.why: Shortest job first maximises throughput but long jobs can be starved.

q.q: Processes A, B and C arrive together needing 5, 3 and 1 ms of CPU time. Round robin is used with a 2 ms time slice. In what order do they finish?
o: A, then B, then C
C, then A, then B
C, then B, then A
B, then C, then A
q.why: A runs 0–2, B 2–4, C 4–5 (finishes), A 5–7, B 7–8 (finishes), A 8–9 (finishes).

q.q: In the same round-robin trace (A 5 ms, B 3 ms, C 1 ms, 2 ms slices), at what time does B finish?
o: 5 ms
8 ms
4 ms
9 ms
q.why: B runs 2–4 ms, then after C (4–5) and A (5–7) it runs 7–8 and finishes at 8 ms.

q.q: Which is a weakness of first come, first served scheduling?
o: One long job at the front of the queue holds everyone else up
Long jobs may be starved because short jobs are always chosen first
Unfinished processes are sent to the back of the queue repeatedly
Urgent events are handled before less important ones
q.why: Processes run to completion in arrival order, so a long job delays all those behind it.

q.q: Why are interrupts more efficient than polling?
o: Interrupts are handled by the device itself, so the CPU never has to be involved
Interrupts stop the current instruction immediately, halfway through execution
Polling saves registers to the hard disk, which is slower than saving to cache
The CPU does not waste time repeatedly checking devices when nothing has happened
q.why: With polling the CPU checks every device whether or not anything has happened; interrupts signal only when attention is needed.

q.q: When does the CPU check whether an interrupt is waiting?
o: At the end of each fetch–decode–execute cycle
Halfway through decoding each instruction
Once every second, using a timer
Only when the computer is started up
q.why: The CPU finishes the current instruction and checks for interrupts at the end of every cycle.

q.q: Which is the correct order for handling an interrupt?
o: Save registers on the stack, run the ISR, compare priority, restore registers
Compare priority, run the ISR, save registers to the hard disk, restore them
Run the ISR, compare priority, save registers on the stack, restore them
Compare priority, save registers on the stack, run the ISR, restore registers
q.why: After checking at the end of the cycle, the priority is compared, registers are pushed on the stack, the ISR runs and registers are restored.

q.q: Where are the register contents, including the program counter, saved while an interrupt is serviced?
o: On the hard disk
On the stack in main memory
In the page table
In the segment table
q.why: They are pushed onto the stack and popped back afterwards, so the original task resumes where it stopped.

q.q: When a file is deleted in most file systems, what happens to its data?
o: It is immediately overwritten with zeros so it cannot be recovered
It is compressed and moved to an archive on the same disk
Its space is marked as free; the data remains until it is overwritten
It is encrypted with the user's key and kept as a backup
q.why: Only the table entries change, which is why deleted files can sometimes be recovered and secure-erase utilities exist.

q.q: What is a device driver?
o: A hardware chip on a peripheral that converts its signals into a form the CPU can use
A program that translates the OS's general requests into commands a specific device understands
A utility that rearranges a disk's clusters so that each file is stored contiguously
A cable standard that lets a device be plugged in and recognised automatically
q.why: A driver is software, normally written by the manufacturer for each OS.

q.q: What does print spooling do?
o: Compresses documents so that they print more quickly
Encrypts the data sent between a computer and the printer
Stores print jobs on disk and sends them to the printer one at a time
Loads the correct printer driver when a printer is plugged in
q.why: Spooling queues jobs so users can carry on working instead of waiting for the printer.

q.q: What does it mean when the OS 'buffers' data for a device?
o: It holds data in memory while a slow device catches up
It identifies a new device and loads the right driver
It records logins so that misuse can be traced
It moves unused pages from RAM onto the disk
q.why: A buffer is temporary memory that smooths the difference in speed between the CPU and a slow device.

q.q: Which OS security function would stop a receptionist from opening patient records?
o: A firewall
Logging and auditing
Print spooling
Access rights (permissions)
q.why: Access rights limit each user to the files and settings they need; a firewall filters network traffic instead.

q.q: A school laptop is stolen. Which OS security function keeps its stored data unreadable?
o: Encryption of the whole drive
Logging of user logins
A firewall filtering traffic
Automatic security updates
q.why: Encrypted data cannot be read without the key, even if the device is lost or stolen.

q.q: Which file management job does the file allocation table support?
o: Filtering network traffic into and out of the computer
Recording where each file is stored on the device and finding free space
Choosing which process runs next on the processor
Translating print requests into printer commands
q.why: The file manager records where each file's data is and finds free space for new data.

q.q: What is a utility program?
o: Application software that helps the user complete a specific task such as writing a report
Part of the kernel that allocates memory and processor time to each running program
System software that performs a specific task to help manage, maintain or protect the computer
A translator that converts source code into machine code for a particular processor
q.why: Utilities look after the computer itself, not the user's own work.

q.q: Which of these is a utility program?
o: Web browser
Payroll package
Spreadsheet
Disk defragmenter
q.why: A defragmenter maintains the computer; the others help users do tasks.

q.q: Why are utilities such as backup and defragmentation often scheduled to run overnight?
o: So they run regularly without being forgotten or interrupting users
Because licences only allow utilities to be run outside office hours
Because they need the processor to run at a reduced clock speed
Because they can only access files when no user is logged in
q.why: Housekeeping is repetitive; scheduling ensures it happens without slowing the system during the day.

q.q: Why is data compression classed as a utility rather than an application?
o: Compression is always built into the kernel of the operating system
Shrinking a file is a means to save storage and transfer time, not a task wanted for its own sake
Compression creates new documents for the user to edit and share
Compression is always lossy, so it must be controlled by the system
q.why: It serves the system's efficiency rather than being the user's goal in itself.

q.q: Which need is met by a disk checker or system monitor?
o: Recovering deleted files from an off-site backup
Defending against viruses and other malware
Diagnosing and repairing problems, such as finding bad sectors
Recovering space by removing unused files
q.why: Disk checkers mark bad sectors and system monitors show which process is using memory or CPU.

q.q: What does a disk defragmenter do?
o: Removes temporary and unused files so that the disk has more free space available
Copies every file to an off-site location so that it can be restored after a failure
Marks bad sectors so that the file manager will not write any new data into them
Rearranges data so each file's clusters are contiguous and free space is gathered together
q.why: Contiguous clusters reduce read/write head movement and so reduce access time.

q.q: Why should a solid state drive NOT be defragmented?
o: It has no moving head, so there is no speed gain, and the extra writes cause wear
It stores every file contiguously already, so the utility would delete data
It is always compressed, so defragmenting would make the files lossy
It holds the OS in ROM, which a defragmenter would overwrite
q.why: Fragmentation slows only mechanical disks; SSDs are managed with TRIM instead.

q.q: What is the main difference between a backup and an archive?
o: A backup removes files from the live system; an archive leaves the originals in place
A backup is a current copy for recovery; an archive stores data no longer in daily use
A backup is made once when data is retired; an archive is updated every night
A backup is always compressed; an archive is always stored uncompressed
q.why: Backups protect live data and stay current; archives retire old data, usually freeing live space.

q.q: Which metadata might an advanced archiving tool store with each file?
o: The page table used when it was last open
The CPU clock speed of the computer that made it
The user's browser history
Its timestamps and access control list
q.why: Metadata such as names, lengths, timestamps and access rights lets each file be rebuilt with its original properties.

q.q: Why might a backup be unreliable even though it runs every night?
o: It is stored off-site, so it cannot be reached when the data is needed
It uses incremental copies, which can never be restored in practice
It has never been test-restored, so nobody knows it can actually be recovered
It is kept current, so it always contains the same errors as the original
q.why: The notes stress that a backup that has never been test-restored cannot be relied on.

q.q: Why are backups usually stored off-site or in the cloud?
o: So the backup files can be compressed with lossy methods to save money
So a fire or theft at the main site does not destroy both the originals and the copies
So the backup software does not need to be scheduled on the main computer
So the data is removed from the live system to free up local storage
q.why: Keeping copies away from the originals protects against site-wide disasters.

q.q: A firm must keep closed client files for seven years but no longer uses them. Which utility is most appropriate?
o: Archive software
Disk defragmenter
Incremental backup
Firewall
q.why: Archiving stores data no longer in daily use for the long term, with metadata, and frees live space.

q.q: Which translator converts assembly language mnemonics such as LDA and ADD into machine code?
o: Compiler
Interpreter
Linker
Assembler
q.why: An assembler mostly produces one machine instruction for each assembly instruction.

q.q: Which translator stops at the first error it finds?
o: Compiler
Assembler
Interpreter
Optimiser
q.why: An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time and halts on an error; a compiler reports all errors together.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a compiler for a company selling a software product?
o: Errors are reported one at a time as the program runs
The executable can be shipped without revealing the source code
The program is translated again every time it runs
Customers need the source code and a translator to run it
q.why: Customers receive only the executable, so the source code stays private.

q.q: Why is an interpreted program usually slower to run than a compiled one?
o: Each statement is translated at run time, every time the program runs
The interpreter optimises the code more thoroughly before running it
Interpreted programs must be converted into assembly language first
The interpreter reports all syntax errors before the program starts
q.why: A compiled program is already in machine code; an interpreter translates as it goes.

q.q: What is the correct order of the stages of compilation?
o: Syntax analysis, lexical analysis, semantic analysis, optimisation, code generation
Lexical analysis, semantic analysis, syntax analysis, code generation, optimisation
Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation, optimisation
Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, code generation, semantic analysis, optimisation
q.why: Tokens are made first, then checked against the grammar, then for meaning, before code is generated and optimised.

q.q: In which stage of compilation are comments removed, tokens made and a symbol table built?
o: Syntax analysis
Semantic analysis
Code generation
Lexical analysis
q.why: Lexical analysis splits the source into tokens and records identifiers in the symbol table.

q.q: During compilation, a variable is used before it has been declared. Which stage detects this?
o: Semantic analysis
Lexical analysis
Syntax analysis
Optimisation
q.why: Semantic analysis checks meaning, such as declaration before use and compatible types; syntax analysis checks grammar.

q.q: What is the main benefit of compiling C# or Java to intermediate code?
o: The program is encrypted so that nobody can ever reverse-engineer it
The program becomes open source and can be modified by anyone
The same compiled file runs on any platform that has the virtual machine or runtime
The program no longer needs any translation at all before it runs
q.why: Bytecode or CIL is processor-independent; a JVM or .NET runtime interprets it or compiles it just in time.

q.q: Which best defines application software?
o: Software that manages memory, devices and processor time
Software that lets the end user carry out a specific task
Software that maintains and protects the computer itself
Software that translates source code into machine code
q.why: Applications serve the user's task; system software serves the computer.

q.q: Why is generic software usually cheaper per user than special purpose software?
o: It is always open source, so no licence fee is charged for it
It needs no operating system, so less code has to be written
It is never updated, so there are no maintenance costs to cover
Its development cost is shared among a very large number of buyers
q.why: Mass-market sales spread the development cost thinly.

q.q: A garage uses a package designed only to book MOT tests and record their results. What type of software is this?
o: Special purpose software
Generic software
A utility program
System software
q.why: It is built to meet one particular business need.

q.q: A dairy farmer uses a spreadsheet only for VAT returns. How should the spreadsheet be classified?
o: Special purpose, because the farmer uses it for only one task at the moment
Generic, because it was designed for many tasks even though it is used for one here
Special purpose, because it is used in one sector, which is farming
A utility, because it helps the farmer manage the business's finances
q.why: The test is what the software was designed for, not what one user happens to do with it.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of generic software for a specialist job?
o: It costs more per user because few buyers share the cost
It can only be used for one task without modification
It may need templates, macros or workarounds to fit the job
It is built around the job with the sector's own terms
q.why: Generic packages are not designed around a particular job; special purpose software is.

q.q: Why is off-the-shelf software usually cheaper than custom-built software?
o: It has fewer features than custom-built software
It is never updated after it is first released
It is always written by volunteers for free
Its development cost is spread across many buyers
q.why: Many customers share the cost; with custom-built software one client pays for all of it.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of custom-built software?
o: Rivals can buy exactly the same package
It contains many features the client never uses
It may lack a feature the organisation needs
Little help is available online from other users
q.why: Only one organisation uses it, so there are no forums or tutorials; the others are off-the-shelf drawbacks.

q.q: Why might custom-built software be less reliable than off-the-shelf software when first used?
o: It has been tested by only one client, so rare bugs may appear later
It is built from many unused features that cause conflicts
It must be configured by the organisation before use
It has been tested by thousands of users with different needs
q.why: Off-the-shelf software is tested by thousands of users; bespoke code may fail under rare conditions, e.g. the first leap year.

q.q: Which situation most favours custom-built software?
o: A shop that needs a standard till package next week
A start-up needing an email service by tomorrow
An organisation with unusual processes, a large budget and time to wait
A small charity with no IT staff and a tight budget
q.why: Unique needs justify the high cost and long development time.

q.q: What is 'tailored' off-the-shelf software?
o: Software written from scratch by a client's in-house developers
A standard package configured or extended with add-ons for one client
Software given away free with its source code available
A web application that runs entirely on the vendor's servers
q.why: It sits between the extremes, giving much of the fit at a fraction of the cost.

q.q: Which point could give an organisation a competitive edge from custom-built software?
o: It is available immediately from many suppliers
It has been tested by thousands of other users
It can do things that rivals' software cannot
Trained staff are easy to find in the job market
q.why: Rivals can buy the same off-the-shelf package, but not the organisation's own bespoke system.

q.q: What makes Windows and macOS different platforms, even on similar processors?
o: Each OS uses a different keyboard layout and screen resolution
Each OS provides a different application programming interface (API) to programs
One of the operating systems uses RAM and the other does not
Each OS needs a different web browser to display web pages
q.why: Programs call OS services through the API, which differs between operating systems.

q.q: Which is an advantage of downloaded and installed software over web-delivered software?
o: No installation is needed on any device
Updates are applied once centrally on the server
It runs on any device that has a modern browser
It works without an internet connection once installed
q.why: Installed software runs on local resources; the other options are advantages of web delivery.

q.q: Why are web applications described as cross-platform?
o: They run in any modern browser on any operating system
They are compiled to bytecode and run by a JVM
They are installed from each platform's app store
They are written in the assembly language of each processor
q.why: Most processing is on the server and the browser provides a common environment.

q.q: A firm's staff use many different devices in several locations. Which is the best reason to choose a web-delivered application?
o: Each device must meet a minimum specification, so performance is guaranteed everywhere
Data is stored on each local device, so it never leaves the building for any reason
The software works fully offline, so staff without a connection can still use it
Updates are applied once on the server, so every member of staff always uses the latest version
q.why: Web delivery gives central updates and access from any browser; local data and offline use are features of installed software.

q.q: Which task is better suited to installed software than to a web application?
o: Editing high-resolution video
Booking a room through a shared calendar
Submitting a holiday request form
Reading a company news page
q.why: Demanding tasks such as video editing, CAD and games need the device's own processing power.

q.q: What is software as a service (SaaS)?
o: Software sold once and installed on each device
Web-delivered applications paid for by subscription
Open source software supported by a community
Utilities that are built into the operating system
q.why: SaaS is the business name for subscription-based web applications.

q.q: What is the defining feature of open source software?
o: It is always free of charge to obtain and to use
It runs only on the Linux operating system
Its source code is available and may be modified and redistributed
It is written entirely by unpaid volunteers
q.why: Freeware is free too; access to and freedom to change the source code define open source.

q.q: How does freeware differ from open source software?
o: Freeware can be modified freely but must not be shared with others
Freeware always costs money after a short free trial period
Freeware's source code is not available, so it cannot legally be modified
Freeware is released under a copyleft licence such as the GPL
q.why: Freeware is proprietary: free to use, but closed and restricted by its licence.

q.q: What does a copyleft licence such as the GNU GPL require?
o: Users must pay the original author a fee for every copy of the program that is made
Users are not allowed to read the source code or reverse-engineer the program
The software may only be used by charities and educational organisations
Distributed modified versions must also be released with their source code on the same terms
q.why: Copyleft keeps derivatives open.

q.q: A small business has no IT staff. Why might it choose proprietary software over open source?
o: It values professional support and a polished, well-documented interface
It wants to change the source code to suit its own processes
It wants to avoid being locked in to a single vendor
It wants to avoid paying any licence fees
q.why: Without in-house programmers the business cannot exploit source code, but a vendor's support line is valuable.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of proprietary software?
o: Several competing versions, called forks, may exist
The organisation is locked in to one vendor for fixes, features and pricing
Documentation is often poor or missing
Support comes mainly from community forums
q.why: If the vendor stops support it ends; the other options describe open source drawbacks.

q.q: When evaluating open source software, what does 'total cost of ownership' include besides the licence?
o: The price of the source code itself
Copyleft fees paid to the original author
Training, migration and support costs
The cost of buying a freeware licence
q.why: Free software can still cost money to adopt, train staff on and support.

q.q: Which is a feature of batch processing?
o: Each transaction updates the master file immediately as soon as it occurs
A guaranteed response time is required for each input from a sensor
An operator must supervise the job throughout to deal with each record
Transactions are collected and processed together at a scheduled time without intervention
q.why: Batch collects transactions into a transaction file and processes them later as one job.

q.q: What is the main drawback of batch processing?
o: An operator is needed throughout the whole run
The master file is out of date until the batch has run
Transactions cannot be validated before processing
Powerful duplicated hardware is always required
q.why: Updates wait for the scheduled run; batch is otherwise cheap and efficient.

q.q: In batch processing, what is a control total used for?
o: To check that no transaction has been lost, duplicated or mis-keyed
To decide which transaction should be processed first
To encrypt the transaction file before it is stored
To guarantee the response time of a real-time system
q.why: Control and batch totals confirm the batch was processed completely and accurately.

q.q: Before a transaction file updates the master file in batch processing, what is usually done to it?
o: It is validated and sorted into the same order as the master file
It is encrypted and sent to each customer for checking
It is compressed with a lossy method to save storage
It is split into threads so each record is processed in parallel
q.why: Validating and sorting lets the master file be updated efficiently in one pass.

q.q: Why must a cash machine use real-time processing?
o: Real-time processing is cheaper because it uses off-peak computer time
Cash machines are offline, so transactions must be stored until night
The same calculation must be applied to every customer's account
The balance must be checked and reduced at once so the customer cannot overspend
q.why: A delay would allow withdrawals beyond the balance.

q.q: Which is an example of real-time control rather than real-time transaction processing?
o: Withdrawing cash from an ATM
Buying a concert ticket online
Traffic lights responding to sensors
Booking a seat on a train
q.why: Control systems must respond to sensor input within a guaranteed time.

q.q: Which application is best suited to batch processing?
o: Booking concert seats online
Producing monthly payroll for all employees
Running a hospital heart-monitor alarm
Withdrawing cash from an ATM
q.why: Pay is needed only monthly and the same calculation applies to every employee.

q.q: A supermarket's sales update stock levels immediately, but reorders are sent at the end of the day. Which processing is used?
o: Both: real-time for stock updates and batch for reorders
Batch only, because reorders are only made once per day
Real-time only, because every sale updates the stock file
Real-time control, because scanners act as sensors
q.why: Sales update the master file immediately; reorders are collected and processed together.

q.q: At a point of sale terminal, which is processing rather than input?
o: Weighing apples on the scales
Tapping a contactless card
Scanning a barcode
Looking up the price in the product database
q.why: Look-up is processing; the others capture data.

q.q: Which smartphone component detects that the phone has been turned to landscape?
o: GPS receiver
NFC chip
Accelerometer and gyroscope
Microphone
q.why: Motion sensors detect orientation and movement.

q.q: Which ATM item is an output?
o: PIN keypad
Receipt printer
Card reader
Checking the balance
q.why: The receipt is produced for the user; the keypad and card reader are inputs and the balance check is processing.

q.q: During an ATM withdrawal, which of these is processing?
o: Typing the PIN on the keypad
Dispensing notes from the cash dispenser
Checking the balance and daily limit, then deducting the amount
Inserting the card into the card reader
q.why: Checking and updating are processing; keypad and card reader are input, the dispenser is output.

q.q: What does EFTPOS stand for?
o: Electronic file transfer protocol over SSL
Electronic funds transfer at point of sale
Encrypted funds transaction for point of sale
Electronic funds transfer of personal savings
q.why: EFTPOS payment uses a card reader or contactless pad, with details sent to the card issuer for authorisation.

q.q: Which is an example of smartphone processing?
o: Combining GPS and compass data for navigation
The vibration motor alerting the user
The microphone recording a voice note
NFC making a contactless payment
q.why: Sensor fusion is processing; the microphone is input, and vibration and NFC payment are outputs.

q.q: Which answer would earn credit for an ATM output?
o: The ATM gives the customer money
The ATM checks the customer's PIN
The keypad shows the amount entered
The cash dispenser outputs the notes
q.why: Answers must be specific and correctly classified; 'gives money' is too vague and PIN checking is processing.
